PM · ABC listen

China eases stance over US spy plane

Broadcast Friday, 6 April 2001 · Reporter: Tom O'Byrne

← Full PM episode — Friday, 6 April 2001

MARK COLVIN: After nearly a week of diplomatic chest beating, signs tonight that the United States and China have both eased up a little on the rhetoric, and maybe ready for a little compromise.

Very shortly now on Hainan Island, US military attache Brigadier General Neil Sealock [phonetic] and a team of diplomats are expecting to have their second access visit with the crew of the American spy plane.

Permission for the meeting was given this morning, a sign of some relaxation in Beijing's line, after previous implications that visits would depend on Washington saying sorry.

There's still a big question over the type of visit the Chinese will allow. On their first contact, the US diplomats were not allowed to talk privately with the airmen and women.

I'm joined from Beijing by our correspondent Tom O'Byrne. Tom, do you know exactly what kind of a visit this is going to be. Is it going to be supervised like the last one.

TOM O'BYRNE: Mark, there's every indication that it'll be no more than that. There is every indication - from the people we've been speaking to - and remember that this is just still very, very early days in this, what seems to be a protracted stand-off - we don't know how long the meeting will go. As you pointed out, we don't whether this meeting will be supervised. We don't even know the purpose of this meeting.

A meeting on diplomatic terms is very, very easy for China to allow. The wider sign or question of release that the Americans want pressed, has not even been mentioned. So at least, in incremental terms, the two sides are talking at least, but there is still a long, long way to go before we're actually seeing these 24 crew members leaving China.

MARK COLVIN: What kind of pressures are there in China on the leadership. I understand that they're in a sense trying to keep a lid on the, the bubbling nationalism that this incident has, has sparked.

TOM O'BYRNE: There has to be a comparison with the quite aggressive encouragement of protests in the streets of two years ago, when the Chinese Embassy - in Kosovo was, in Belgrade was bombed. And these were mass orchestrations in the streets - particularly around the American Embassy where bus loads of university students were given time off lectures to actually protest outside the Embassy, the Consulates right across mainland China.

In contrast this time those efforts by the students - and there is considerable anti-China, anti-American sentiment that is always in the, in the undercurrent here in China, but that sentiment is being tamped down by very, very effective policing and control - whether it be on campuses or outside the American Embassy.

MARK COLVIN: It's still bursting out on the Internet though isn't it.

TOM O'BYRNE: That's right. That's, that's at least one way that people are venting their concern and their frustration and their anger at what they see - and this is a very palpable anger - about what they see as Americans spying on China.

But the, the indication from the Internet and from the chat rooms, is at least it gives rise to a support for the strong Chinese stand by the leadership. But at least on the campuses there is every indication, from the people we've been speaking to, that any efforts at organisation by the students, is quickly stamped out.

We've only seen - just in the last 12 hours - some efforts by Chinese police just outside the American Embassy, to move on protestors - the sporadic number of protestors that there have been.

MARK COLVIN: The sub-text to the diplomacy has been that the Chinese have been using trade as a lever, as a bargaining chip with the Americans, because they know that the Americans have got such a vast amount of money and such a vast amount - politically and economically - invested in their relationship with China.

But it's a two edged sword isn't it. I mean the, the Chinese are exporting $40 billion worth of goods to America, and they could hardly afford to lose that either.

TOM O'BYRNE: I think both sides, deep down, realise that this is a fight that no-one wants, that neither the Americans nor the Chinese want, and indeed, none of the trilateral partners that each of these sides have in this region or indeed right across the world wants either.

And there is considerable lobbying from embassies for example in Beijing here, on the sidelines of this, pressing the international case for this incident to be solved quickly and smoothly and without further escalation.

MARK COLVIN: But aren't we getting quite close now to the point where the Chinese will find themselves no longer dealing with just the Bush administration. This is going to start spreading, and they're going to be dealing with an angry public, and that means an angry Congress, which can exert all kinds of revenge on them - whether it be over the World Trade Organisation or even putting pressure on the Olympic organisation not to let them have the Olympics in 2008.

TOM O'BYRNE: Well on that point, there is already an impact being felt on both sides of the Pacific. We're hearing that a delegation from one of the biggest States in the United States has cancelled a business delegation here to China that was supposed to arrive this weekend.

The leader of that delegation was saying, in all conscience, he could not turn up with his delegation and begin to do business with China while there were 24 crew members on the ground in Hainan Island. Very much for domestic consumption in the United States no doubt, but still an impact nevertheless.

There is another delegation that is pending. Their 22 members, a big representation from the United States, that's supposed to arrive here this weekend.

The Chinese stock market plays in, on NASDAQ and on Wall Street are significantly down on their figures from last week. So that these, these are having . this incident is having a practical and immediate impact and I, but I think that we mustn't forget the fact that there is sufficient pressure and sufficient calmness around the edges of this particular dispute, to try and contain it to this simple incident of a plane landing on Hainan Island, as difficult as that might be to understand.

MARK COLVIN: Tom O'Byrne thank you. And no doubt we'll be talking to you about this early next week as well. It's difficult to see it going away just over the weekend.
